accident_report:
Vehicle initialization

On a straight one-way downhill road with three lanes, numbered from right to left as lane 1 to lane 3, the pavement is wet but visibility is good, and there is a wide shoulder to the right of lane 1. V1 is in lane 2, traveling at 82 km/h in a steady car-following state, with the intent of continuing straight downhill while maintaining a safe following gap. V2 is 45 m ahead of V1 in the same lane, traveling at 84 km/h, also moving steadily and intending to continue straight with speed coordinated to the surrounding flow. V3 is in lane 3, positioned about 8 m behind the left rear of V1, traveling at 80 km/h, holding its lane and intending to continue straight alongside the traffic stream. V4 is in lane 1, about 12 m behind the right rear of V1, traveling at 86 km/h, and intends to move forward more aggressively than the coordinated flow in the adjacent lanes.

Scene development

As the vehicles continue downhill on the straight segment, the coordinated speeds of V1, V2, and V3 keep the traffic flow stable, and the safe following distance between V1 and V2 leaves a visible but legitimate buffer in lane 2. Because the road is downhill, V4 closes the distance from lane 1 slightly faster than the other vehicles. V4 then uses the wide shoulder on the right to extend its path, with its right wheels crossing onto the shoulder, and immediately makes an illegal cut-in toward lane 2, aiming for the gap between V1 and V2. Since visibility is good, all drivers can clearly see the maneuver, but the problem is not detection; it is that V4 enters the gap at only 74 km/h, noticeably below the coordinated speed of the traffic stream.

When V4 completes the cut-in, it leaves only about 18 m to V2 ahead and about 16 m to V1 behind. V2 responds first by braking from 84 km/h to 76 km/h to rebuild distance from the newly inserted V4. V1, now facing a much smaller headway to a slower vehicle on a wet downhill surface, brakes harder, reducing speed from 82 km/h to 58 km/h. This braking action from V1 directly affects V3: V3 sees V1 decelerating sharply and shifting slightly left within lane 2 as if preparing for an evasive maneuver, so V3 brakes from 80 km/h to 62 km/h and holds position in lane 3 instead of moving forward. As a result, V3 occupies the left-side escape space that V1 might otherwise have used.

At the same time, V2’s reduction to 76 km/h directly affects V4, because V4 has cut in too close and now has even less room in front. V4 is forced to brake again, from 74 km/h to 64 km/h, to avoid hitting V2. That second speed drop further compresses the gap behind it. V1 continues heavy braking on the wet surface, but the downhill grade lengthens the stopping distance, and the available distance is no longer sufficient. V1 cannot steer left because V3 is still alongside and has already closed that escape option by maintaining its position after braking. V1 also does not return right because V4’s cut-in path originated from the shoulder side and the immediate conflict remains directly ahead in lane 2. The combined effect of the downhill grade, wet pavement, initially coordinated traffic speed, the legal safe following gap that V4 exploited, and V4’s illegal low-speed cut-in turns a stable multi-vehicle flow into a rapidly collapsing chain of interactions.

Result

The scene ends with the first collision occurring in lane 2: V1’s front strikes the rear of V4 after V1 is unable to shed enough speed on the wet downhill roadway. The involved vehicles in the first collision are V1 and V4. No later impacts are considered.
